contributions.headingText: Sialoblastoma is a low-grade malignant primitive salivary gland anlage neoplasm.
2B67.Y & XH0G00 Other specified malignant neoplasms of parotid gland & Sialoblastoma
Not recommended: embryoma; basaloid adenocarcinoma; congenial basal cell adenoma; congenital hybrid basal cell adenoma–adenoid cystic carcinoma.

Tumours arise most commonly in the parotid gland (in two thirds of cases) followed by the submandibular gland, with only rare reports in minor salivary gland sites {17178498; 24163547; 27284424; 17638426; 31257547}.

Patients present with painless facial swelling, with rare cases showing nerve involvement or skin ulceration {1965332; 10078927; 14674095; 16818073; 24163547}. Other tumours (naevi and hepatoblastoma) may be coexistent {16049999; 16514617; 10890938; 9159361}. Elevated AFP has been reported {16049999}.

Imaging

This lesion is usually diagnosed in the neonatal period but is occasionally seen on antenatal imaging.
The vast majority of tumours are identified at birth or within the few months of life, with only rare reports in adults. There is no sex predilection {24163547; 29728174}.
The tumour may originate from retained blastema cells rather than basal reserve cells {27284424}.

Tumours are lobulated, well defined, and encapsulated, or they may show infiltration into the surrounding tissue. The cut surface is usually grey or yellow and solid. Tumours range from 15 to 150 mm in size. Focal haemorrhage or necrosis may be present {3211816; 3029739; 3725707}.

Sialoblastoma typically exhibits solid organoid nests composed of primitive basaloid epithelial cells, separated by dense fibrous stroma. Tumour cells have indistinct cell borders, scant cytoplasm, a high N:C ratio, and round to oval vesicular nuclei with occasional nucleoli. In addition, differentiated budding ducts lined by cuboidal to columnar epithelium with intraluminal basophilic secretions or a cribriform pattern may be present. Peripheral nuclear palisading is occasionally present. Tumour cells may exhibit apoptosis, necrosis, and nuclear pleomorphism, with increased mitoses. Tumours are not graded.

Immunohistochemistry

By immunohistochemistry, tumours are reactive for SOX10, p63, nuclear β-catenin, and KIT (CD117), and variably reactive for cytokeratins including CK5/6, CK7, and CK19, along with SMA and calponin {32695659}.

Differential diagnosis

The primitive histological features and the young ages of patients help to differentiate sialoblastoma from other basaloid salivary gland tumours such as basal cell adenoma/adenocarcinoma, adenoid cystic carcinoma, and adamantinoma-like Ewing sarcoma {18926196; 27327192; 29728174; 11210851; 30285997; 32695659}.

Aspirations are often not tolerated by infants. When performed, smears are cellular and show arrangements of tight, solid sheets or clusters of basaloid cells with scant cytoplasm, round to oval vesicular nuclei, and occasional nucleoli. The cellular clusters may contain ductal cells and dense, metachromatic, magenta hyaline globular material with smooth, rounded outlines {26214398; 14674095}.

Essential: primitive, solid, organoid nests; basaloid epithelial cells with vesicular chromatin; cuboidal to columnar ductal cells.

Desirable: dividing fibrous stroma; peripheral palisading.
Sialoblastoma is staged using the TNM system as published by the Union for International Cancer Control (UICC).

Local recurrence is seen in about one third of patients, and regional and distant metastases are seen in about 15% {27368441}. Death from disease is rare {11090328; 16818073; 24163547; 27368441; 29728174; 31257547}. A less aggressive behaviour is suggested for tumours in the submandibular gland versus other anatomical sites. Histological features associated with a worse prognosis include tumour necrosis and increased mitoses or a high Ki-67 proliferation index.
